entry.title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Review: Sylvester Stallone’s Wild Hollywood Underdog Story Gets a Punchy Crowdpleaser
entry.summary: Peter Farrelly continues his reign of making audience-delighting hits for the TIFF crowd, but this one pulls its punches a bit. 'I Love Rocky' review.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 13, 2026 at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Amazon MGM Studios will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6, before going wide on Friday, November 20.]

You’re going to see the hits coming with this one. When Anthony Ippolito first utters the title of Peter Farrelly‘s “I Play Rocky” — it’s an admission and an ask, a demand and a plea — the moment is primed for stand-up-and-cheer crowd-pleasing. Such is the case with Farrelly’s entire film, which tracks Sylvester Stallone’s wild, improbable Hollywood success story through the lens of his creation of “Rocky,” often functioning as its own version of that underdog story, presumably because “Rocky” proper isn’t available to be remade and Stallone was not formally involved with the production of this one.

Related Stories
IndieWire’s Trevor Wallace Wins Daytime Emmy for Editing ‘IndieWire Craft Roundtables’
‘The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins’ Is the Funniest Series of the Year

Stallone has long mythologized his rise to greatness, and that’s no knock on him; his rise to Hollywood royalty was crazy and filled with eye-popping twists and turns. The guy sold his dog when he didn’t have enough money! But Peter Gamble’s script sands down those hard edges into something much more made-for-the-movies, a distinctly knotty treatment for a movie that is meant to be about how hard it is to get original movies made.

While the lightness of the film — including an awkward dinner in which Frank Stallone, Jr. (Matt Dillon) giddily admits to beating his kid, mostly played for chuckles — can detract from the much darker stuff that really happened to Stallone, it’s hard to deny the power of a feature so genuinely built to delight. You can see the strings being pulled (the ropes being strung?), but that means it works more often than not. With a big crowd — a man behind me at the film’s second public screening at TIFF guffawed and hooted with such abandon throughout the film that I could only embrace his joy — “I Play Rocky” does exactly what it’s trying to do.

It doesn’t do much more, though.

Stallone’s life story has been threaded through the period just before he started writing scripts and the opening night of “Rocky,” an essential time in the career of a man so dedicated to acting and his craft that it could have ruined him forever. And there’s some light ruin here, including a short stint sleeping on the street (we see literally one night), bonkers financial decisions, and grievous financial choices. Embodied to an almost disarming degree by actor Anthony Ippolito — most people are probably going to get hung up on his impersonation of Stallone’s signature voice, but I’ve never seen anyone make their cheekbones look like Sly’s unexpectedly sunken ones — what feels most real about the film exists because he’s so fully committed to the bit.

And it’s very much to the breakout star’s credit that it doesn’t feel like a bit. While Gamble’s script doesn’t get much further than “this dude just really loved acting,” Ippolito gets pretty soulful here. His Sly (or, as we first meet him during a run of demeaning auditions, “Mike”) is a striver who would likely never call himself “ambitious.” Self-taught, self-educated, and self-aware to a fault, Sly knows he’s not the ideal Hollywood star, but he’s hellbent on showing the world what he’s got.

When his eventual first wife Sasha (a wonderfully calm AnnaSophia Robb) encourages him to just “write a fricking script” worthy of his talents, he does. The first is not “Rocky.” Neither are the seven that follow, but Sly and Sasha still pull up stakes for Hollywood and to chase his dream. No one is buying what he’s selling, though, and even some promising meetings (including one with Irwin Winkler and Robert Chartoff, both played to the absolute hilt by P.J. Byrne and Toby Kebbell, respectively) end nowhere. A chance encounter — the film’s script lives and dies by those — with a seminal boxing match gives him fresh inspiration, and after just three days, the kid has “Rocky.”

But is he going to be Rocky? Of course, everyone on Earth who sees this film (and plenty who don’t) knows that answer, but what the film lacks in tension, it makes up for in pure grit. Sly learns all about Hollywood negotiations, blustery studio men (a role Tracy Letts was born to play; no one has more fun yelling “Fuck Paramount!” than this guy), and holding fast to seriously deluded dreams. And while the film can flag as we chug through those paces, once “Rocky” is greenlit with Sly in the lead role (and a mess of stipulations, all of them seemingly designed to trip him up), things really start zipping along.

Part of that is due to smart casting. Jay Duplass is a stellar pick for director John G. Avildsen, though anyone who knows anything about Stallone’s on-set approach will chuckle at how much these two seemed to get along (Stephan James should get his own Carl Weathers film now). But more of it comes from the film’s eventual bent toward the mechanics of moviemaking. Come for the high jinks involving beating back union reps (but also, ew?), stay for a subplot about the genius of the Steadicam that is genuinely moving to observe.

That “Rocky” will be a hit is a given — and a fricking huge one at that! — but “I Play Rocky” is far more invested in getting the audience on board with the road it took to get there. And while Farrelly’s approach to this material, extremely glossy and built to delight a wide array of audience members, doesn’t quite speak to the real pain that went into the making of “Rocky,” there’s still plenty here that will make people stand up and cheer. It would, however, be nice if this Hollywood story didn’t feel quite so, well, Hollywood.

Grade: B-

“I Play Rocky” premiered at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Amazon MGM Studios will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6, before going wide later in the month.

entry.title: IndieWire’s Trevor Wallace Wins Daytime Emmy for Editing ‘IndieWire Craft Roundtables’
entry.summary: IndieWire's Trevor Wallace has won a Daytime Emmy for editing our IndieWire Craft Roundtables series.
entry.content:
IndieWire’s Trevor Wallace is officially an Emmy winner.

Wallace won the Editing for a Daytime Studio Program category at the 53rd annual Daytime Emmys for his work on Season 1 of “IndieWire Craft Roundtables.” He accepted the award during the ceremony at the Hollywood Palladium on Friday, October 30.

IndieWire was also nominated for a Daytime Emmy for Outstanding Directing for a Daytime Studio Non-Fiction Series for IndieWire executive producer Mary Pelloni’s work on the show. The two nominations and one win, in categories that also included broadcast talk shows, reflect IndieWire’s increasing presence in the traditional video spaces in addition to our written coverage.

Related Stories
‘The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins’ Is the Funniest Series of the Year
Netflix Will Give Joel Coen’s Gothic Mystery ‘Jack of Spades’ a Theatrical Release in 2027

Wallace works on IndieWire’s staff as a video producer, where he also produces and edits video content across brands like Filmmaker Toolkit, Future of Filmmaking, and other editorial and sponsored projects.

Season 1 of “IndieWire Craft Roundtables” highlighted the below-the-line artisans on many of the biggest films of the season. Hosted by IndieWire’s Jim Hemphill, the season consisted of four episodes, each centered around a different filmmaking department: cinematography, editing, production design, and casting. Each episode aired on PBS SoCal and streamed on the PBS App in addition to editorial coverage on IndieWire.com.

Wallace won for the editing roundtable episode, which featured included editors Kirk Baxter (“A House of Dynamite”), Affonso Goncalves (“Hamnet”), Michael P. Shawver (“Sinners”), Andy Jurgensen (“One Battle After Another”), Pamela Martin (“Springsteen: Deliver Me from Nowhere”), Saar Klein (“Dead Man’s Wire”), and Luke Lynch (“BLKNWS: Terms & Conditions”).

The cinematography roundtable featured Adolpho Veloso (“Train Dreams”), Malik Hassan Sayeed (“After the Hunt”), Michael Bauman (“One Battle After Another”), and William Rexer (“The Testament of Ann Lee”).

The production design roundtable featured conversations with Cara Brower (“Hedda”), Sam Bader (“The Testament of Ann Lee”), Alexandra Schaller (“Train Dreams”), Scott Chambliss (“Kiss of the Spider Woman”), and Dylan Cole and Ben Procter (“Avatar: Fire & Ash”).

The casting roundtable also featured casting directors Nina Gold (“Jay Kelly”), Margery Simkin (“Avatar: Fire & Ash”), and Jessica Ronane (“After the Hunt”).

“IndieWire Craft Roundtables” returned for Season 2 in June 2026, with six episodes devoted to the biggest TV shows of the year.

entry.title: ‘The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins’ Is the Funniest Series of the Year
entry.summary: The "30 Rock" team has made something new while adhering to their joke-dense, pop-culture savvy, and network-friendly approach to sitcoms.
entry.content:
When I first thought, “Is ‘The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins’ the funniest show on television?”, I worried saying as much would be damning the uproarious NBC sitcom with faint praise. After all, the modern TV landscape is awash with crime shows, genre mash-ups, and I.P. brand extensions. Bad comedies abound (and tend to be mercifully easy to spot), but great ones? Hmm. At least the most recent Emmy winner for Best Comedy Series is an actual comedy, but the nominees (including a feel-good weeper, a rom-com heavy on the rom, and that cooking drama) were still emblematic of a Hollywood era when laughs aren’t the top priority.

Related Stories
As Production Jobs Flee California, Governor Gavin Newsom Pushes to Expand Film and TV Tax Credit to $1 Billion Annually
‘Who Killed Alex Odeh?’ Review: A Scattered but Searing Documentary Examines America’s Tacit Acceptance of Anti-Arab Discrimination

So, returning to the original question, how many funny funny shows actually came out this year?

Turns out, quite a few. “Adults” jumps to mind among recent releases for its successful Season 2 evolution into a hang-worthy Gen-Z hangout sitcom. “Colin From Accounts” capped a three-year run that saw the Aussie romantic-comedy get stronger every season. “Youth” has Sharon Horgan back at the top of her game (let’s not speak of “Bad Sisters” Season 2), and “The Comeback” did the impossible by delivering a worthy successor to one of HBO’s greatest-ever TV seasons. Then there’s trusty comedy staples like “It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia” and “Abbott Elementary,” which don’t need another crossover to keep us laughing, as well as the half-comedies that feel full to anyone with the same funny bone, like “The Lowdown” (a noir comedy), “The Audacity” (a black-comic drama), and “Trying” (a family comedy). I didn’t even mention the final season of “Hacks” (which is great) or the first (and hopefully final) season of “The Hawk” (which is not).

“Reggie Dinkins” tops them all.

Following fallen NFL running back Reggie Dinkins (Tracy Morgan), decades after he’s ousted from the league for gambling, Season 2 picks up amid incremental progress toward his crowning redemption: making the Pro Football Hall of Fame. His documentarian, Arthur Tobin (Daniel Radcliffe), is still searching for the right angle to support their comeback film (Arthur needs it as much as Reggie wants it), while Reggie’s agent and ex-wife Monica (Erika Alexander) tries to build on the little momentum they gained at the end of last season (when Reggie earned his first votes ever).

The irresistible ensemble doesn’t have a weak link. The staging is vibrant. The writing is as happy to delve into topical subject matter (like documentary subjects paying their documentarians) as it is to revel in carefree absurdity (like a harebrained murder-conspiracy or calamitous Thanksgiving gathering). And every element of it is always focused on being funny. Not only is Robert Carlock and Sam Means’ NBC sitcom designed to squeeze in as many jokes as the human brain can process in 21-minute chunks, it’s also carefully paced and polished to keep those jokes as superb and surprising as possible.

Take a check-your-phone-and-you’ll-miss-it gag from the Season 2 premiere: Monica is struggling to keep up with the media landscape’s sprawling marketing opportunities and admits she booked Reggie on the wrong show: She mixed up Pablo Torres’ sports podcast with Julio Torres’ “something.” Quick cut to Julio (as himself) interviewing Reggie about “the color clear.” There’s a laugh in recognizing Monica’s mistake, another laugh in Julio’s question (“What do you think about the color clear?”), and another laugh in Reggie’s response (“A lot!”).

But rather than one joke stepping on the next, they amplify one another. Monica’s explanation is given the most space to land, since technically it’s setting up the cutaway jokes to come. Those jokes hit one after the next, but in a rhythm that makes them easy to process independently. They’re calibrated to keep you laughing all the way through, but they’re not so rushed that you feel overwhelmed instead of entertained.

That’s the magic (or maybe the math) behind what’s recognized as Tina Fey (an EP on “Dinkins”) and Robert Carlock’s comedy style, as established by their landmark sitcom, “30 Rock” and extended more successfully than not in comedies like “Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt” (where they picked up Radcliffe), “Great News,” “Mr. Mayor,” and “Girls5Eva.” Carlock continues it here with Means, who worked on all those shows, while relying on their proven bonds with Morgan, Radcliffe, and stealth MVP Bobby Moynihan to maintain the right balance. (Moynihan’s understanding of tone and timing is impeccable, and he’s such a joyful presence it’s hard not to smile whenever Rusty surfaces.)

The Season 2 premiere illustrates the trust the writers’ have in their entire acting company. The story still pivots around Morgan’s lovable doofus, but the emphasis is elsewhere. Arthur is dying for the family to find out about Reggie’s son Carmelo (Jalyn Hall) and his secret relationship with Delilah Basmati (Arica Himmel), daughter of Reggie’s nemesis, Jerry Basmati (Craig Robinson). Brina (Precious Way) gets close, while Monica is busy hiring a new assistant “head of publicity” to help her tap into younger markets with a broader reach. Moynihan’s Rusty is everywhere, chipping in enough quips, reaction shots, and physical comedy to convey his supportive yet integral presence in each character’s life.

By the time our original dynamic duo gets a cathartic moment near the episode’s end, it’s hard not to notice that Reggie and Arthur almost feel like an afterthought — and that’s just fine. They take back control in the ensuing episodes, after “The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins” proves it can thrive no matter who gets to press the most buttons. The joke-delivery machine is operating at peak volume, and it needs every capable hand to keep its performance at the same incredible sweep.

With only four episodes screened for review, there’s plenty of time for Season 2 to break down. The charming vibe could fade, the sharp jokes could soften, the elastic performances could calcify. But not only does Carlock and co.’s lengthy track record suggest the opposite trajectory, so does the excitement shown in creating this specific project. You can feel it in the ideas, big and small, throughout “The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins,” and their cumulative impact makes the series special — not because of a general dearth in great comedies, or even because it harkens back to an era of Must-See TV, when multiple classic sitcoms airing on the same night spoiled viewers with an abundance of laughs. It’s just because laughing this hard, this often, is a gift. And there’s nothing faint about it.

Grade: A-

“The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins” Season 2 premieres Monday, November 2 at 8:30 p.m. ET on NBC. New episodes will be released weekly and made available on Peacock the next day.

entry.title: Netflix Will Give Joel Coen’s Gothic Mystery ‘Jack of Spades’ a Theatrical Release in 2027
entry.summary: The film stars Patsy Ferran, Josh O’Connor, Damian Lewis, and Lesley Manville.
entry.content:
Joel Coen is heading back to Netflix. After taking his 2021 “The Tragedy of Macbeth” to A24, the filmmaker is bringing his latest solo directorial outing back to Netflix, where he last teamed with brother Ethan Coen on the 2018 release “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs.” Rest assured, however, while Ethan is not sharing directing duties with his big brother again, he did co-write the film‘s script alongside Joel, novelist and screenwriter Eleanor Catton, and playwright and screenwriter Conor McPherson.

The new film is called “Jack of Spades,” and the streamer will give it a theatrical release in the fall of 2027 ahead of its debut on Netflix. The film is based on Frances Frederica Montrésor’s 1901 novel “The Alien: A Story of Middle Age” and its official logline reads: “A sinister gothic mystery filled with intrigue and betrayal set in the atmospheric Scottish Highlands.”

Related Stories
As Production Jobs Flee California, Governor Gavin Newsom Pushes to Expand Film and TV Tax Credit to $1 Billion Annually
‘Earthlings in Love’ Review: A Sentimental Sci-fi Journey Makes the Leap from TikTok to the Tokyo International Film Festival

The film will star Olivier Award winner Patsy Ferran, BAFTA nominee and Golden Globe winner Josh O’Connor, BAFTA nominee and Golden Globe winner Damian Lewis, and Oscar nominee Lesley Manville.

The book itself is billed as “a thoughtful pick for readers who enjoy character-driven fiction with a touch of wanderlust and a battle between integrity and longing.” Montrésor’s novel follows Esther Mordaunt, “now well into her thirties by the story’s start” and “follows her evolving bond with Jasper, a traveler with a vivid past and a talent for storytelling. Through his tales of sailing, revolutions, and distant lands, the book explores how a single life can stretch across time, risk, and longing without losing its humanity.”

Coen will also reunite with Oscar-nominated cinematographer Bruno Delbonnel (“Inside Llewyn Davis”) and composer Carter Burwell (“Fargo,” “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs”). The film will be produced by Robert Graf, Frances McDormand, Coen, Steven Rales, Graham Broadbent, and Pete Czernin, and executive produced by Donald MacKinnon.

entry.title: As Production Jobs Flee California, Governor Gavin Newsom Pushes to Expand Film and TV Tax Credit to $1 Billion Annually
entry.summary: As California production jobs dry up, Gov. Newsom pushes to expand film and TV tax credit from $750 million to $1 billion.
entry.content:
Governor Gavin Newsom is proposing expanding California’s current film and television tax credit program from $750 million to at least $1 billion annually as the state is struggling to attract entertainment industry jobs. The move comes as a report last month by FilmLA found that production levels fell 3.7 percent in the third quarter even as California has continued to enhance its tax credits. Many of the major studios and streamers are headquartered in Los Angeles, which makes the contraction in production jobs more painful.

Last year, Gov. Newsom pushed to increase California’s film and TV incentive from $330 million to $750 million annually, and the state’s film commission saw an initial rise in applications before the number of productions began falling again. California is not only grappling with increased competition from states like New Jersey, New York, and Georgia that offer richer incentives, but they are also facing off against foreign production hubs such as the United Kingdom and Hungary.

Related Stories
‘Earthlings in Love’ Review: A Sentimental Sci-fi Journey Makes the Leap from TikTok to the Tokyo International Film Festival
Ruth Madeley Never Thought Acting Was an Option — Now, She’s Playing a Disability Rights Legend in ‘Being Heumann’

In a press release, Gov. Newsom said the proposed expansion would include credits for above-the-line talent, as well as rewards for companies that commit to fielding more than one production in California. If enacted, the tax credit will be extended through 2040, which would give companies more certainty about the incentives they can access. The previous incentives were scheduled to last through 2030. It would also increase independent film funding to $100 million annually, up $26 million from the current program.

“California created the modern entertainment industry; we’re the capital of entertainment and we’re going to keep it here,” Newsom said in a statement. “At least $1 billion in tax credits means more investment flowing into our economy and more opportunity across the industry. Through this expansion, we will maintain the momentum and success of our historic expansion last year.”

The governor also urged national lawmakers to pass a federal film and television incentive, which could augment states’ efforts to bolster local production.

“States can’t shoulder the cost alone, which is why I am calling on Congress to back up an expanded tax credit by passing national film and TV tax credit legislation already on the table,” Newsom said.

entry.title: ‘Earthlings in Love’ Review: A Sentimental Sci-fi Journey Makes the Leap from TikTok to the Tokyo International Film Festival
entry.summary: “One Cut of the Dead” director Shinichiro Ueda helms a project that’s better than a “vertical drama” has any right to be.
entry.content:
It’s a queasy proposition for cinephiles: Take a TikTok series, retrofit it into a feature film, and premiere it at a major international film festival. But that’s exactly what happened with “Earthlings in Love,” the latest project from Japanese director Shinichiro Ueda. It’s the first so-called “microdrama” (also known as a “vertical drama”) to premiere at the Tokyo International Film Festival, an unusual choice given that in Japan, as abroad, these short-form videos are designed for casual viewing on smartphones, not the formal atmosphere of a film festival. “Earthlings in Love” was originally released in 30 parts on social media, then recut for its TIFF debut; this version is significantly longer, going from a 76-minute runtime to an 102-minute one. It’s also — and this is crucial — much better than anyone might expect, given its provenance.

Related Stories
Ruth Madeley Never Thought Acting Was an Option — Now, She’s Playing a Disability Rights Legend in ‘Being Heumann’
Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Beats ‘Clayface’ to Capture First Place

It’s not terribly surprising that Ueda in particular would be open-minded about working in a new media format: His “One Cut of the Dead” broke out internationally in large part because of its ingenious approach to low-budget storytelling. “Earthlings in Love” is similar in that it takes its limitations and turns them into strengths, thoughtfully incorporating the vertical-video format both into the film’s mise en scene and its structure. It would be disingenuous to say that you forget about the vertical framing after a while — I certainly didn’t — but Ueda makes the most of the tight 9:16 aspect ratio, shooting dialogue scenes from the waist up and composing shots so that they move the eye upwards rather than across the frame.

Even more clever is the way that Ueda, who also wrote the script, incorporates the feeling of claustrophobic disconnection into the story itself. This is a movie about selective memory, centered on a fortysomething film director named Shinpei (Kato Shinsuke) whose career has been prematurely halted by early-onset dementia. Returning to his hometown for the funeral of a former classmate, Shinpei tries to recall why he and his friends never finished their zero-budget high-school sci-fi opus, “Earthlings in Love.” Shinpei remembers a dramatic classmate quitting the shoot because he felt the movie was beneath him, and his secret crush encouraging him to keep going. But is that what really happened?

That’s what we see in the first 20 minutes or so of the movie, as Ueda blends “Rashomon” with “Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind” by having Shinpei consult a service that offers to recover his fading memories by feeding photos and diary entries into an AI-generated recreation of his own past. As we find out, the AI is reflecting Shinpei’s own faulty recollections back to him; Ueda insists that this isn’t a commentary on AI per se, but it does bring to mind the way that LLMs create feedback loops that have led to the pop-psychological phenomenon of AI psychosis. Luckily for him, Shinpei has Nagisa (Kiyose Yaeko), another former classmate with whom he reconnected on his trip back home, to keep him grounded in the present. Her role in Shinpei’s life is unclear at first, not least because he keeps forgetting where he knows her from. Over time, however, she becomes the story’s most tragic figure.

As with “One Cut,” the plot structure of “Earthlings in Love” is built on a series of dramatic twists. This is where Ueda puts the “microdrama” format to its most ingenious use, revisiting moments we’ve already seen from new perspectives that reveal important pieces of information previously left out of the frame. Simply by panning a few feet left or right, Ueda can completely change the narrative and emotional stakes of the film. And the way he applies this technique feels fresh and genuinely innovative, not to mention organic to a potentially offputting new style of storytelling.

The story itself is not as fresh, leaning on themes of high-school nostalgia and missed connections that are common in Japanese popular cinema. However, they’re given an earnest, if sometimes overly sentimental, airing here thanks to Ueda’s personal connection to the material. The director has not been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s, but he was a prolific amateur filmmaker beginning in junior high, and the flashback scenes of “Earthlings in Love” are set in the year 2000, when Ueda was a sophomore in high school. The fact that this ‘00s nostalgia piece was made via a very 2020s model of filmmaking is just further evidence of Udea’s casual formal brilliance.

These scenes are not the only ones that ring true, however, as Kato and Kyose successfully carry the plot through outrageous coincidence and into three-hanky tearjerking. “Earthlings in Love” aches for a lot of things, chief among them the simple joy of creating something with your friends just for the fun of it. Its core message is ironic, given the disposable nature of its initial release: Human memories fade, but movies are forever. Now that it’s a proper film, its lifespan has a better chance of being extended.

Grade: B+

“Earthlings in Love” premiered at the 2026 Tokyo International Film Festival. It is currently seeking U.S. distribution.

entry.title: Ruth Madeley Never Thought Acting Was an Option — Now, She’s Playing a Disability Rights Legend in ‘Being Heumann’
entry.summary: 'Being Heumann' star Ruth Madeley talks to IndieWire about playing a disability rights activist in Siân Heder's Oscar-contending movie. Interview.
entry.content:
Ruth Madeley originally thought she’d become a screenwriter, attending Thornleigh Salesian College where she studied English and creative writing with an emphasis on scriptwriting. “I wanted to be a storyteller,” “Being Heumann” star Madeley told IndieWire. “It’s not that I didn’t want to be an actor, or I didn’t pursue it. I didn’t even think it was an option.” And it’s easy to understand why. Born with spina bifida and growing up as a wheelchair user, Madeley was aware that disabled actors, and roles written for them, weren’t exactly plentiful. “I never saw anyone who looked like me,” she said. “So to even know that that was potentially an option was madness to me.”

Related Stories
Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Beats ‘Clayface’ to Capture First Place
Producer Titles Can Be Bought, but Real Creative Producers Take Them for Themselves

When Madeley thinks back on some of the earliest disabled representation she saw in popular culture, her answer is similar to countless other disabled film and TV lovers: it was an abled actor playing a disabled part. “There’s a soap back at home where there was a wheelchair user, and I was like, ‘Oh, his wheelchair looks like mine.’ And then I found out the actor wasn’t a wheelchair user.” With that type of representation being the norm, it’s unsurprising that Madeley saw acting as something she was barred from. That is until 2009, when “Half Moon Investigations,” a children’s crime/comedy show, needed a wheelchair user for an episode. “I auditioned purely to be nosy and extend my network, and I got the role. I remember being terrified in the audition, thinking: ‘Why do people do this? This is awful,” she said in an interview with The Guardian earlier this year.

That role kickstarted a film and television career that has flourished over the last decade. Now, Madeley is the star of “Being Heumann,” which details the life of disabled activist Judy Heumann and the 504 sit-ins in 1977. It’s a performance that could not only make history if she and the movie are Oscar-nominated, but also finally give young disabled girls someone who looks like them onscreen. Something Madeley didn’t have growing up. “As a disabled person, being aware that you might make history, that’s huge for me,” she said. “It’s huge for the community. That’s a really heavy and exciting thing to have.”

But Madeley doesn’t want that history, or getting caught up in the discussion of representation, to overshadow the film’s content. “I’m not just a random wheelchair user they pulled off the street,” Madeley said. “This is my job, so talking about the actual craft is really exciting for me.”

And that craft was multifaceted. Not only was Madeley portraying an actual person, a legend in the disabled community. She also had to do accent work, ASL work, and appear in nearly every frame of the movie. The accent was particularly important to get right, as Heumann’s Brooklyn upbringing was a huge part of her life, and indicative of her prickly personality. “I don’t find [accents] easy,” she said. “I have to work at them, and learn the science of it, and the tongue placement. All of those interesting fun things that I get to play with. She was such a proud Brooklyn woman, I wanted to be able to sound so specifically like her.”

That specificity was imperative to Madeley in every aspect of playing Heumann. “Siân [Heder, director] and I spoke so much about movement, because we’ve been so starved of seeing disabled people on screen that you don’t always see how a disabled person moves through the world.”

Both Heder and Madeley were intrigued by the juxtaposition of Heumann’s desire for movement with her paralysis forcing her to be still. “Siân and I both were fascinated by Judy’s speed and freedom when she was in her chair; she was never still,” said Madeley. “Versus when she’s out of her chair, and she is in such a different state of vulnerability.”

The sequence in the trailer, where Judy is forced to wait for her in-home health attendant to show up so she can use the restroom, makes this painfully apparent. “Once she was in bed, she had all of these pillows, and she knew that she had to be comfortable when her attendant left because the second that attendant left she couldn’t move herself for the whole night.”

It was seeing the authentic lived experience of a disabled person, activist aside, that was so compelling to Madeley. “The worst thing I can watch on screen is if something looks too easy,” said Madeley. Too often movies made after the passage of the Americans With Disabilities Act present a rose-colored view of accessibility, or at least do so by never discussing it. Here, the movie authentically details what being a wheelchair user, a blind person, or a deaf person was like in 1977. The landscape is riddled with different access barriers, both individually and societally. But Heder and the production team made a point of showing all of those, not just the stairs crafted to enter buildings, but putting the wheelchair-using cast in actual wheelchairs from the 1970s.

“The 1970s chairs helped [with authenticity] because nothing is easy in those things for anyone,” said Madeley. “There were so many people on hand to help, which was so invaluable because even if the place was fully accessible, being in those chairs makes things so much harder. They weighed so much. Why did people keep them? That’s what I don’t get.”

Because the wheelchairs were so unwieldy, the actors needed to get out of them to relax their bodies. It was also a chance for Madeley to realize her own limitations as a disabled person, and remember that no two disabled people have the same experience. “I recognize my privilege. I’m an ambulatory wheelchair user. I can stand up and stretch if I need to. There were other people that couldn’t… So that was a learning curve as well throughout the process of filming. People need to get out of these every few hours.”

On the page, Heumann isn’t sanded down, and Madeley is happy with that. “I’m all for a messy queen!” Her Judy is impatient, stubborn, downright rude at times. But Madeley wanted to make sure that was placed alongside Heumann’s joy, warmth, humor, and vulnerability. Without that delicate balance, the character could have come off as too bitter, on one end of the spectrum, or too tragic.

“That feeling of having to be easy, or grateful, or nice, so that people — all of those things that society expects of a disabled woman–I’m not those things all the time, and no one is,” she said. “I love the fact that I got to play somebody who didn’t have her edges rounded off. I love the fact that she was able to be prickly.”

In the end, Madeley wants to keep showcasing flawed humans, not necessarily flawed disabled humans. “I’m just driven by character,” she said. Too often, disabled actors are only hired for disabled roles, and that’s something Madeley wants to subvert. “I don’t only have to play disabled. I can play the messy mom of two who’s got knocked up again, and who is completely inept.” Madeley continues to show that the different sides of disability will no doubt finally turn the tide on what disabled actors can do. It’s a far cry from the type of representation she, and many other disabled people, had growing up.

“Being Heumann” opens from Apple TV in select theaters starting Friday, November 6. The film streams on Apple TV starting Friday, November 13.

entry.title: Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Beats ‘Clayface’ to Capture First Place
entry.summary: 'You Can See Everything' takes first place at the box office, crosses $60 million domestically.
entry.content:
“You Can See Everything,” A24’s buzzy documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, has narrowly defeated Warner Bros. and DC Studios’ “Clayface” at the domestic box office. It added $10.6 million to bring its haul to $63.9 million. That was good enough for a first-place finish, something that “You Can See Everything” pulled off for the first time in its third weekend of release.

“Clayface,” a body horror “Batman” spinoff, earned $10.4 million, bringing its North American gross to $44.1 million. The superhero adventure has earned $83 million globally. It cost $44 million to produce, a relatively inexpensive figure for a comic book adventure. The film is part of James Gunn and Peter Safran’s efforts to revitalize DC and make it a true competitor to Marvel. The duo’s first film, “Superman,” was a hit when it debuted in 2025, but “Supergirl” lost tens of millions and was excoriated by critics last summer.

Related Stories
Producer Titles Can Be Bought, but Real Creative Producers Take Them for Themselves
Michael Mann Accidentally Shoots Himself in Leg at Los Angeles Gun Range

Laika’s stop-motion film “Wildwood” earned $7.5 million to push its domestic total to $25 million and its global gross to $35 million. The film is adored by critics but carries a $100 million price tag, which means it will struggle to climb into the black.

Black Bear’s erotic dramedy “Wicker” earned $4.1 million from 2,374 theaters in its second weekend to push its domestic tally to $13.2 million. The studio bought the film out of Sundance for $2.5 million, so it stands to be a modest hit for the company as it gets into distributing its own movies.

Elsewhere, “Everest: The Other Side,” the new documentary from the “Free Solo” team of Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin, debuted in limited release with $1 million from 515 locations. National Geographic Documentary Films backed the picture, which is expected to be an awards contender. Another Oscar hopeful, Sony Pictures Classics’ “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” expanded its footprint this weekend, earning just over $1.9 million from 1,112 screens. That brings its domestic haul to just over $2.1 million. The indie studio is pushing John Turturro for a long-overdue Academy Award nomination.

After this weekend, “You Can See Everything” has supplanted Michael Moore’s “Bowling for Columbine” to become the 18th highest-grossing documentary of all time. It cost a mere $7 million to produce.

entry.title: Producer Titles Can Be Bought, but Real Creative Producers Take Them for Themselves
entry.summary: Producers Alison Owen, Carla Hacken, and Lauren Miller Rogen tell IndieWire about the importance of persistence in bringing films and TV shows to life
entry.content:
As part of the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking team presents “Behind Their Lens,” a series of panel discussions with some of the most exciting artisans, directors, and producers of 2026.

On the producers panel, “Tangles” producer Lauren Miller Rogen, “Ghosts” and “Harlots” producer Alison Owen, and “Devil Wears Prada” producer Carla Hacken spoke to students and guests about everything from how they approach giving good, productive notes on a story to how they’re looking at the current, rapidly consolidating media landscape for actually getting projects off the ground.

But the thing that unites all their work, across all phases of production, is a persistence to muscle it past whatever obstacles and challenges lie in its path. And that’s something that’s been true for them since they got into the actual work of the producing business. Owen spoke about how her “degree” in producing is something she earned with a bunch of university students, but not by actually attending university. It just started with a conversation with someone who was attending the UK’s National Film School at the time.

Related Stories
Michael Mann Accidentally Shoots Himself in Leg at Los Angeles Gun Range
The Arcane Knowledge Directors Wish They Could Summon

“This was the early ‘80s, when things were a lot looser, but they said, ‘There are no producers there. But if you want to learn about producing, go to Notting Hill, where the bus stops outside the Coronet in the morning and just stand there and get on the bus,” Owen said. “You would get out to the film school, and the students who were making their graduation films would want someone to come out and produce for them. And they didn’t care that you hadn’t done anything. I didn’t know what a call sheet was or what PAs were or anything. But they were happy to have a pair of hands.”

Being a willing pair of hands led Owen to a small village in the middle of Wales, working on a senior graduation project, and that on-the-ground, very-on-location work has stood her in good stead since. “Not only are you learning stuff, but you’re meeting your peers. So they were all people who wound up directing major studio movies, editors, cinematographers, people that I work with now, like John Mathieson, who — you know, we all slept on a mattress above a pub, and he now lights for Joe Wright,” Owen said. I always say to students, ‘Network with your peers. They’re the people of the future that you’re going to want to get jobs from or hire.”

Being tuned into what your peers are up to can also show you what’s possible. Miller Rogen had written the script for her first feature, “For A Good Time, Call…” years before, but it was seeing Lena Dunham’s work in “Tiny Furniture” that made her realize it was something she could make happen herself.

“I saw ‘Tiny Furniture,’ and I thought, ‘Well, I could do that.’ And so I took the movie from the big producer, and I emailed my team and my writing partner, and I said, ‘We’re gonna make this on our own, and I’m gonna star in it.’ And they were like, ‘Whoa.’ And I was like, ‘No, that’s what we’re doing,’” Miller Rogen said.

That conviction — and the key connections to some independent backers care of Miller Rogen’s brother who worked in finance — led to a $750,000 raise for the film’s budget. “We shot in 16 days. And then we went to Sundance, which is, of course, lucky to get into. But we got into Sundance and Focus Features bought it and released it, and it was in movie theaters, which would never happen now. But it was extraordinary, and I felt shock and pride and fear because it was gonna be big and out there,” Rogen Miller said. “But it was incredible, and I think these days, there are so many ways to get your project seen.”

“ I think you just said the most important thing for all of them is there’s so many ways for you guys to get your work out there now,” Hacken added. “The success of ‘Backrooms’ and all these YouTube horror shows should give you hope that, you know, write something good, produce something good, find a great story, and there are other ways to get it made than the way it used to be.”

entry.title: Michael Mann Accidentally Shoots Himself in Leg at Los Angeles Gun Range
entry.summary: Michael Mann is in stable condition after accidentally shooting himself in the leg.
entry.content:
Michael Mann, the director of “Heat” and “The Insider,” shot himself in the leg at a Los Angeles gun range on Saturday.

A spokesperson for the filmmaker said that “a weapon accidentally discharged while holstered resulting in a superficial injury.” Mann was treated at a local hospital for a wound that was subcutaneous and minor. He is being released. The event took place during target practice. Mann is an experienced shooter who has been practicing on ranges for decades.

A spokesperson for the Los Angeles said that officers had responded to a “shots fired” incident at The Range LA at roughly 4 p.m. An investigation determined that the shooting was “accidental.” TMZ broke the news of the shooting.

The 83-year-old Mann is known for directing gritty crime stories, many of which look at cops and criminals and are set in urban landscapes. He was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Director for his work on the 1999 journalism thriller “The Insider” and the film was nominated for Best Picture. Mann’s other credits include “Thief “(1981), “Manhunter” (1986), “The Last of the Mohicans” (1992), “Ali” (2001), “Collateral” (2004), and “Public Enemies” (2009). As a producer, Mann received an Oscar nomination for Martin Scorsese’s 2004 drama “The Aviator.”

Mann’s most recent credit was 2023’s “Ferrari” and he is about to shoot a sequel to “Heat” that is based on a novel he co-wrote with Meg Gardiner. That film will star Christian Bale, Leonardo DiCaprio, and Stephen Graham. Mann also helped create the ’80s TV hit “Miami Vice” and later directed a film version of the show.

entry.title: The Arcane Knowledge Directors Wish They Could Summon
entry.summary: As part of SCAD Savannah Film Fest's Behind Their Lens panel, directors told IndieWire about the areas of filmmaking they'd love to explore more of.
entry.content:
As part of the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking team presents “Behind Their Lens,” a series of panel discussions with some of the most exciting artisans, directors, and producers of 2026.

On the directors panel, “Blue Heron” writer/director Sophy Romvari, “Josephine” writer/director Beth de Araújo, “Custom of the Country” director Josie Rourke, “The Good Daughter” director Steph Green, and “Toy Story 5” co-director Kenna Harris spoke about their different paths into directing — a fair amount of team sports — and how they approach everything from thinking about locations to communicating their vision clearly with different members of their crews.

Related Stories
Artisans Break Down the Tricks and Treats of Designing a Trojan Horse at SCAD Savannah Film Festival
What Genre Will Be Hollywood’s Next Big Trend? Watch IndieWire’s ‘Pitch Me’ Panelists Weigh in

But the panel also spoke about the ways in which film as a medium is constantly changing and skills they would like to be able to bring to future projects, and that all directors might want to be aware of.

Rourke, whose first feature film had the challenge of creating a sweeping historical scope for “Mary Queen of Scots,” has been thinking about how directors and visual effects artists can work better together since she had to drop some (digital) castles into some Scottish hillsides.

“I just knew it wasn’t working, but I couldn’t figure it out. And in the end, I called a friend of mine who’s a really good architect and said, ‘Listen, just pop into the edit,’ [to look at the castle assets], and he looked and went, ‘Yeah, that wouldn’t stand up,’” Rourke said. “It was really interesting because my body had a visceral fear of wanting to use that structure. It’s just an imaginary castle but [I knew] it was dangerous.”

Rourke’s instinctive awareness is something she’s since worked on trying to better communicate with VFX teams, but there’s even more nuance to how those discussions are had. “Some of the smoke and mirrors about [VFX choices] is about cost. So I don’t even know how to look at this and go, ‘Here’s how I would achieve that more economically,’” Rourke said. “I know how to cut costume or cut set or cut script or cut the schedule, but I don’t know how to be in dialogue that is sensibly and creatively managing the budget for visual effects.”

Harris, who has been embedded in the world of digital animation for years as a story artist before fusing into a hivemind with their fellow co-director Andrew Stanton to tackle “Toy Story 5,” still has things about the process they want to learn, too.

“I wish I understood simulation a little bit better because I want to learn how to talk about in a way that feels more collaborative. And the reason I say that is because there are certain things that even today in a really fancy studio like Pixar that are still hard to crack, visually,” Harris said.

One of those things is folds in clothing — the ability to create the sense of clothing moving along a character’s body naturally or bunching up around the elbow in a believable way, the seemingly simple but actually quite complicated to craft illusion of a hood lying against someone’s shoulders.

“If I was gonna say, ‘Hey, I really care about sleeve folds,’ I’m sure my producer, Lindsey Collins, would be like, ‘What? Why? Why, why would you care about that?’” Harris joked. “But artistically, I’m fascinated by it. We’re still relying on these physics-based engines for things like that, and when I look at a lot of 2D art, there are people who can design the hell out of just making clothing [work], it’s beautiful the way that cloth works on our bodies, and it’s just so hard to do on a feature scale. And so, I think it would be awesome if I understood simulation more technically because then maybe I would get closer to having a conversation of finally getting to see the sexy clothes folds that I’ve wanted my whole life.”

Clothing is something that’s both important and underrated in live-action, too. For as much and as proudly as “Blue Heron” is an indie film, it was the first time that Romvari had worked with a costume designer and saw the power of what having a creative collaborator in that department could do.

“It’s often seen as this very frivolous and just clothing and, you know, often is treated as just like a woman’s department and who really, you know, just put something on them. But I’ve learned so, so much through working with my costume designer, Maria [Katarina], how integral it is for continuity, aesthetically, but also for actors’ safety and comfort,” Romvari said.

Costume does a lot of silent work in “Blue Heron” since it is a period piece set in the late ‘90s (horrid thought) with sections taking place in a more contemporary timeline as well. The shift in clothing, and how characters feel about themselves through how comfortable they are in their clothes, articulates things that they themselves can’t quite say.

“Just so often costume designers are asked, ‘Can you just throw something on them?’ And now I understand the inner turmoil that they go through when they’re like, ‘Do you know how much time I spent dying that shirt and then using this artificial scrub to make it look like it’s from this other period?’ Just so much work goes into it that’s just not respected, and it’s so integral to what you see on screen,” Romvari said. “ So I think I’m just speaking up for costume designers. It’s a really important element that I think is undersung for its value.”

entry.title: Artisans Break Down the Tricks and Treats of Designing a Trojan Horse at SCAD Savannah Film Festival
entry.summary: Production designer Ruth de Jong, editor Sarah Broshar, and costume designer Amy Roth talk about the hidden touches they put into their crafts.
entry.content:
As part of the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking team presents “Behind Their Lens,” a series of panel discussions with some of the most exciting artisans, directors, and producers of 2026. On the artisans panel, “The Odyssey” production designer Ruth de Jong, “Paper Tiger” and “I Play Rocky” costume designer Amy Roth, and “Disclosure Day” editor Sarah Broshar spoke to students and guests about their process and approaches towards each of their particular corners of the giant puzzle that is putting a film together.

But there was one thing that united all of them, across their different creative disciplines, and that was the importance of (sometimes quite literally) climbing hilltops to create a sense of authentic surprise.

Related Stories
What Genre Will Be Hollywood’s Next Big Trend? Watch IndieWire’s ‘Pitch Me’ Panelists Weigh in
Watch the ‘Rehearsals for a Revolution’ Director and Editor Explain How Memories Can Help Fight Authoritarianism

If a costume designer can delight a director without being asked for something specific, then the movie is alive. If the editor’s intuitive sense of rhythm is working in harmony with the footage that’s been shot, then in a lot of respects the film is showing the post team what it wants to be. And if a production designer can build a Trojan Horse to the right scale and it falls down? Well, don’t panic. It can look even more weathered and accurate to the initial plan when it’s picked back up again.

“Obviously the scale [of the horse] came from me needing to fill it physically with the actors and the IMAX camera and [cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema] and Chris. So that’s how we proportionally worked out and built several of them, then built a separate body of the horse to physically shoot that scene, lowered it into a tank, and shot that on a set near our city of Troy,” De Jong said.

But in addition to needing to half-drown Odysseus (Matt Damon) and his companions, an IMAX camera, cinematographer, and acclaimed director, some of the aspects that make the Trojan Horse truly look like it’s been in the wars came about organically.

“[For the opening], we mounted the horse to a massive trench plate and got a dredger. We dredged up really deep into the sand. We did a few tests a couple of days before. We put the horse in the waves. It took a beating. It fell. We had to rebuild it overnight to then shoot the next day. So the horse you are seeing in the film went through a lot before it got shot. It was very physical,” De Jong said. “Water always wins.”

But according to De Jong, the work of production design, even on projects without the grand scope of “The Odyssey,” is always the same. “ I feel deeply that if my sets are too obvious, I’ve failed because they should fade to the back and the actors should just be immersed in their worlds, and the audience should be lost in that world,” De Jong said.

This is as much the case for good contemporary costume design, where the clothes should just help us make judgments about the characters and feel the shifts in the story, something Amy Roth talked about doing almost invisibly in both “I Play Rocky” and “Paper Tiger.” With the former, Roth took a lot of cues not just from the existing material around “Rocky” and Sylvester Stallone, but about how the character of ‘Mike’ would feel about his body as he worked himself up into becoming Sly.

“He really was like three people,” Roth said. “Dressing him early on was taking hints from a future Sly and putting them in the way he dresses so that we can see the impetus of how ‘Rocky’ came to be. He was big into working out and he was very body conscious. So that silhouette was important to me and I was literally, like, layering clothing onto Anthony so that he couldn’t bulk up,” Roth said.

Meanwhile on “Paper Tiger,” Roth worked in a silent partnership with the sets in order to give the characters caught up in a mob scheme more or less agency. “The house was very beige, so I put the actors just so that the mother was in focus. And then in the end she starts to fade. She starts sort of matching the walls; the mother and father sort of fade into the background.  And that’s just me doing my thing. I don’t think I even discussed that with James [Grey, the director], but he would’ve liked it.”

What the director likes and how the director is responding gets very important in the edit, which is where Broshar’s developed a great read on Steven Spielberg over the course of their many collaborations.

“When you’re spending hours and weeks and months and years sitting in a room with somebody, you get shorthands. You don’t have to say words as much. You can just kind of feel a twitch. If I make a little twitch, Steven will look at me, like, ‘What? What are you thinking?’ You can tell,” Broshar said. “I think you’re just always trying to sit down and watch the movie or watch the scene like you’ve never seen it before. I always watch myself watching something, and I try to see if I’m feeling tense or if I am getting distracted or thinking about what’s for lunch — and that is a real red flag.”

One of the ways in which Broshar can help surprise herself and the other folks watching a cut is with sound, especially on a delightfully bonkers action sequence like “Disclosure Day” has in its train chase. “Like anything, it just takes patience and imagination, and you keep an eye on the timing of things — where and how do you want to see the train, how far away is it, when do we hear the train, how loud is it?” Broshar said. “ I have great assistants who do really good sound work, and I just kept asking them for more. They’d say, ‘We spent three days on this.’ And I’m like, ‘Great. Now spend three more.’ And let’s just keep [going] more, more, more, more. And then, you know, it all gets polished out as soon as great Gary Rydstrom and Bryan Chomier and their team come in with sound.”

Whether it’s sound, color, or the elements of nature themselves, it’s the surprises and flourishes that artisans build into their work that help each filmmaking department feel alive.
